title: Who are the barbarians?
hook: Montaigne asks whether the peoples of Brazil that Europeans call savage are more barbaric than Europe's own wars (Essays 1.31)

segments.voice: Yesterday, a well-made head. Your line was well made, not full. Did you get to understand one thing all the way through, instead of collecting ten? Day one thousand one hundred fifty-two.

A pair of trousers. That's where today's essay lands, on a joke about trousers. To get there, Montaigne travels a long way without leaving home. He starts with a man in his household who had lived for a long time on the coast of Brazil, and who told him about the people there. He moves through what Europeans of his day said about those people. And he ends up back in France, in the middle of its own wars. The question he carries the whole way is today's title: who are the barbarians?
screen: `A JOKE ABOUT TROUSERS.` → `A REPORT FROM BRAZIL.` → `BACK TO FRANCE.`

segments.voice: First, the turn. The essay is called Of Cannibals, and Montaigne says that, from what he's been told, he finds nothing barbarous or savage in these people, except that each of us calls barbarous whatever is not our own custom. Two days ago we met custom making anything look natural. Here the idea gets teeth. Second, the mirror. He doesn't pretend the people he heard about were gentle. He describes them killing enemies in war and eating them. Then he turns around. He says there is more barbarity in eating a man alive than dead: in tearing apart, by torture, a body that can still feel, and roasting it bit by bit. He says he has seen this done, and not among old enemies but among neighbors and fellow citizens, and under cover of piety and religion. He was describing his own country, in his own time. Third, the visitors. Some of these men came to France, and Montaigne records what struck them. They found it strange that so many tall, bearded, armed men would obey a child instead of choosing one of their own to lead. And they had noticed some people stuffed with every good thing while others, whom they called their halves, begged at their doors, thin with hunger. They wondered why the hungry put up with it. Fourth, the trousers. After all this, the essay ends with a shrug in the reader's voice: not bad at all, but so what? They don't wear breeches. Montaigne lets his reader sneer, and the sneer gives the reader away. One honest note: he never went to Brazil. Everything here came secondhand, and he tells us whose hands.
screen: `OUR CUSTOM, THEIR BARBARISM.` · `TORTURE AMONG NEIGHBORS.` · `THE VISITORS' QUESTIONS.` · `THEY DON'T WEAR BREECHES.` · then, large: `WHO ARE THE BARBARIANS?`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: question one us and them. Sit, and let the breath settle on its own. Bring to mind a group you tend to call them. Not the worst group you can think of; an ordinary one. People who vote another way, raise kids another way, eat dinner another way. Find one habit of theirs that looks odd to you. Now turn it around, the way Montaigne does: which habit of yours would look odd from their side of the table? Hold both for a while, without deciding who wins. Let the breath keep going. The bell holds the time.
Who are the barbarians? Montaigne's question in Of Cannibals: each of us calls barbarous what isn't our own custom, and sometimes the cruelty is closer to home. Today's word.
Your line: who are the barbarians. Today, when you hear yourself say those people, ask the question once, quietly, before you finish the sentence. Day one thousand one hundred fifty-two.

howItsDone: Readers of Montaigne often take Of Cannibals as practice in turning a judgment around: before calling another people barbarous, look hard at what your own side does.

myth: Montaigne says the people he heard about never did anything harsh
he describes them killing and eating enemies taken in war, then says torturing the living is worse.
he points to cruelty done by neighbors and fellow citizens in his own time
he says he has seen it, and under cover of piety and religion.
Montaigne sailed to Brazil to see for himself
he never went; he relied on a man in his household who had lived there, and on other reports.

fork.setup: you're Montaigne. you've just written that the people of Brazil eat enemies killed in war. what comes next on the page?
options: a warning to readers about savages.
the cruelties you've seen neighbors do to each other in your own country's wars.
fork.reveal: he turns the lens around: tearing apart a living body by torture, done among fellow citizens under cover of religion, is more barbarous than eating the dead.

original.script: chacun appelle barbarie ce qui n'est pas de son usage
original.say: shah-KUN ah-PELL bar-bah-REE suh kee nay pah duh sohn ew-ZAHZH
original.note: French, Montaigne's own words in Of Cannibals: each person calls barbarism whatever isn't their own custom.

trapdoor: what you thought: Of Cannibals is a travel tale about a faraway people.
what it means: it's a mirror. the word barbarian tells you about the speaker's customs, and the cruelty he calls worse is at home.
what a scholar hears: the portrait of Brazil is secondhand and he says so; the eyewitness part of the essay is the cruelty of France's own religious wars.
recall: a try, a test, an attempt

sources.ref: Essays 1.31, Of Cannibals (each calls barbarous what is not his custom; more barbarity in eating a man alive than dead; torture among neighbors under cover of piety; the visitors' remarks on obeying a child and on their 'halves' begging; the ending about breeches)

notes: All Montaigne is paraphrased; Cotton/Hazlitt is not on the validator's public-domain list and the writer did not rely on its exact wording.
Essay numbering follows the outline (1.31, the Villey/Pléiade numbering); Cotton's edition numbers it 1.30.
Original-language line 'chacun appelle barbarie ce qui n'est pas de son usage' is from memory of the French; confirm wording and pronunciation.
The visitors' 'child' is the young king; the script avoids naming him or giving the city or date of the meeting to keep within the claims rule.
The script calls the people 'the people of Brazil' as the outline does; Montaigne does not name the nation. Some modern readers identify them as Tupinambá; left out.
Days 1142–1151 were not on disk when this was written; the review uses the index line for day 1151.

Editor pass: cut the outside claim that Montaigne was a Catholic writing during the religious wars (not in the cited text; the essay's own 'neighbors and fellow citizens, under cover of piety and religion' carries the point); trapdoor no longer calls the home cruelty 'the worst' (he says 'more barbarous').
